text: Red field with a black double-headed eagle; nothing else looks like it.
Vertical blue-yellow-red with a coat of arms in the centre. Romania has the same bands but no emblem.
Plain red-white-red horizontal thirds. Latvia is a darker maroon with a much thinner white stripe.
Vertical black-yellow-red. Germany uses the same colours as horizontal stripes.
Blue field with a yellow right triangle and a diagonal line of white stars.
Horizontal white-green-red. Hungary is red-white-green and Italy is a vertical green-white-red.
Red-white-blue horizontal with a red-and-white chequerboard coat of arms. Serbia is red-blue-white, and Slovenia is white-blue-red with a small shield.
White field with a copper-coloured silhouette of the island above two olive branches.
White over red with a blue triangle at the hoist. Poland is white over red without the triangle.
White Nordic cross on red, with no inner border. Norway adds a blue cross inside a white one.
Horizontal blue-black-white. Lithuania is yellow-green-red and Latvia is maroon with a thin white stripe.
Blue Nordic cross on white, the only Nordic flag with a white field.
Vertical blue-white-red. The Netherlands uses red-white-blue as horizontal stripes.
Horizontal black-red-gold. Belgium has the same colours as vertical stripes.
Nine blue and white stripes with a white cross in the blue canton. Uruguay also has stripes but with a sun in the canton.
Horizontal red-white-green. Italy is vertical green-white-red and Bulgaria is white-green-red.
Blue with a red cross edged in white. Norway is the reverse: red with a blue cross edged in white.
Vertical green-white-orange. Ivory Coast is the same bands in reverse order, and Italy has red.
Vertical green-white-red with no emblem. Mexico has the same bands plus a coat of arms.
Dark carmine with a narrow white stripe. Austria has equal red and white thirds.
Horizontal yellow-green-red.
Red-white-light blue horizontal. It is the Dutch layout with a lighter blue and a longer shape.
Vertical white-red with a small George Cross in the top-left corner.
Red over white, matching Indonesia in colour. Monaco is much squarer, and Poland is the other way up.
Red with a gold border and a gold double-headed eagle.
Red-white-blue horizontal. Luxembourg has a lighter blue and a longer shape.
Red with a yellow sun whose eight rays spread to the edges.
Red with a blue cross edged in white. Iceland is the colour reverse.
White over red. Indonesia and Monaco have the opposite order.
Green hoist and red fly, with the coat of arms sitting on the border between them.
Vertical blue-yellow-red, almost identical to Chad. Andorra has the same bands but with a coat of arms.
Horizontal white-blue-red with no emblem. Slovakia, Slovenia and Serbia use the same colours with coats of arms.
White over light blue with a coat of arms in the centre.
Red-blue-white horizontal with a large coat of arms toward the hoist. Russia has the white-blue-red order and no arms.
White-blue-red with a shield showing a double cross, set toward the hoist. Slovenia has a smaller shield in the top-left corner.
White-blue-red with a small shield in the upper hoist corner. Slovakia has a larger shield centred on the hoist side.
Red-yellow-red with a thick central yellow band and a coat of arms off-centre toward the hoist.
Yellow Nordic cross on blue. Finland swaps to a blue cross on white.
A white cross on red in a square shape, one of only two square national flags.
Two equal horizontal bands, blue over yellow. Sweden has the same colours but with a cross.
The Union Jack. Australia and New Zealand carry it in the canton alongside stars.
Blue over red horizontal bands with a gold crown in the upper hoist corner.
White field with a red Nordic cross outlined in blue.
White band over a thinner red band, with a red castle and a hanging gold key.
Red field with a three-legged triskelion of armoured legs in the centre.
White field with a red saltire, a red-and-gold badge and a gold crown at the top.
Blue field with a red-bordered yellow Nordic cross, like the Swedish and Finnish colours combined.
A red disc on white, centred. Bangladesh has a green field and an off-centre disc.
White with a red-and-blue taegeuk and four black trigrams in the corners.
Five stripes: red, white, double-width blue, white, red. Costa Rica uses the same idea with a double-width red centre.
Blue-red-blue with a white Angkor Wat temple as the flag’s central emblem.
Red field with a blue canton holding a white 12-rayed sun.
Red over white with a white crescent and five stars in the top-left. Indonesia has no emblem.
Fourteen red and white stripes with a blue canton holding a yellow crescent and star. It resembles the US flag at a glance.
Plain red over white. Monaco matches in colour but is squarer, and Poland has the reverse order.
Blue over red with a white triangle at the hoist holding a sun and three stars.
A yellow lion holding a sword on maroon, beside green and orange vertical stripes.
Vertical red-blue-red with a yellow Soyombo symbol on the hoist stripe.
Sky blue with a golden sun and a soaring eagle, plus an ornamental pattern at the hoist.
Red with a yellow sun in the centre containing a crossed-lines tunduk emblem.
White with two blue horizontal stripes and a blue Star of David.
Black-white-green horizontal with a red triangle at the hoist holding a white seven-pointed star.
A red vertical bar at the hoist beside green, white and black horizontal stripes.
Maroon with a white serrated edge of nine points. Bahrain is similar but has five points and is red.
Red with a white crescent and star. Tunisia places the crescent and star inside a white disc.
Diagonally split yellow and orange with a white dragon across the middle.
Saffron-white-green horizontal bands with a blue 24-spoke wheel (Ashoka Chakra) in the white band.
Dark green field with a red disc set slightly toward the hoist.
Red-blue-red horizontal bands with a large white disc in the blue band.
Red-white-red with a green cedar tree in the centre white band.
Red field with a white five-petalled bauhinia flower.
Green field with a white lotus flower over a bridge and water, under an arc of five gold stars (a large one in the middle).
A green sideways Y with white and yellow edging, a black triangle at the hoist, red above and blue below.
Light blue with a black band edged in white across the middle.
Blue, yellow and crimson bands with a Swazi shield and spears in the centre.
Blue-white-green horizontal with a black Basotho hat in the centre.
Black, red and green stripes with white edging and a Maasai shield with crossed spears.
Six horizontal stripes of black, yellow and red with a crowned crane in a white disc.
Diagonal black band with yellow edges, green in the upper hoist and blue in the lower fly.
Vertical green-white-green with no emblem.
Red-gold-green horizontal with a black star. Senegal uses vertical stripes with a green star.
Vertical green-yellow-red with a green star in the centre.
Red with a white disc holding a red crescent and star.
Blue, yellow and green horizontal bands with a golden sun in the upper fly corner.
White vertical band at the hoist, with red over green horizontal bands to its right.
Thirteen stripes with fifty white stars in the blue canton. Malaysia has 14 stripes and a crescent.
Red-white-red vertical with a red maple leaf. Peru lacks the leaf on its civil flag.
Vertical green-white-red with an eagle on a cactus. Italy has no emblem.
Green with a yellow rhombus and a blue globe.
Greek has letters Cyrillic lacks, such as Σ, Ω, Ψ, Θ and Ξ.
Greek road signs show the Greek name with a Latin transliteration underneath.
Russian uses ы, э and ъ, which Ukrainian does not have.
Russian writes street as "ул." (улица); Ukrainian uses "вул.".
Ukrainian has the letters і, ї, є and ґ, none of which exist in Russian.
Ukrainian writes street as "вул." (вулиця), not "ул.".
Bulgarian uses ъ as a vowel inside words, as in България.
Bulgarian has no ы, э, ђ or ћ.
Serbian Cyrillic has the letters ђ, ћ, џ, љ, њ and ј.
Serbian signs commonly show Cyrillic and Latin spellings side by side.
Macedonian uses ѓ, ќ and ѕ, which Serbian and Bulgarian do not.
Like Serbian, Macedonian uses ј, as in Скопје.
Mongolian Cyrillic adds the vowels ө and ү.
Double vowels such as "аа" and "уу" are common in Mongolian words.
Kyrgyz Cyrillic adds ң, ө and ү to the Russian letters.
Kyrgyz lacks Kazakh letters such as ә, қ and ғ.
Kazakh Cyrillic has extra letters such as ә, қ, ғ and ұ.
Kazakh and Kyrgyz both use ң, ө and ү, but only Kazakh uses ә, қ and ұ.
Thai is written without spaces between words; spaces mark phrase breaks.
Thai letters are rounded, many starting with a small loop.
Khmer stacks consonants beneath each other using subscript forms.
Khmer letters look more ornate and angular than Thai.
Sinhala letters are very round and loop-like.
Sri Lankan signs are often in Sinhala, Tamil and English.
Hebrew is written right to left with separate, squarish letters.
Israeli road signs usually show Hebrew, Arabic and Latin spellings.
Hangul builds square syllable blocks from circles, lines and boxes.
Korean signs often include a Latin romanisation underneath.
Hiragana or katakana usually means Japan, not a Chinese-script country.
Katakana is angular and used for loanwords and foreign names.
Taiwan usually uses traditional Chinese characters with no kana (Hong Kong and Macau do too).
Bopomofo phonetic symbols such as ㄅ and ㄆ sometimes appear on Taiwanese signs.
Arabic is written right to left in connected cursive letters; عمّان is Amman, the capital of Jordan.
Hebrew letters stay separate; Arabic joins them. The script is shared across the Arab world, so the place name is what points to Jordan.
Russian has ы, э and ъ; Ukrainian has none of them.
Russian signs write street as "ул."; Ukraine uses "вул.".
Ukrainian uses і, ї, є and ґ, which Russian lacks.
If you see "вул." for street, it is Ukraine.
Serbian Cyrillic has ђ, ћ, џ, љ, њ and ј; Bulgarian has none of them.
Serbian signs often pair Cyrillic with a Latin line; the letter ј is a quick giveaway.
Bulgarian uses ъ as a vowel inside words, e.g. България and Търново.
Bulgarian lacks ђ, ћ, џ, љ, њ and ј.
Macron vowels ā, ē and ī appear only in Latvian; ū is used in both Latvian and Lithuanian.
Latvian also has ģ, ķ, ļ and ņ with a comma mark below, which Lithuanian lacks.
Lithuanian has ą, ę, į, ė and ų; Latvian has none of them.
Many Lithuanian place names end in -ai or -iai, such as Šiauliai.
Czech has ř and ů, which Slovak does not.
Czech writes street as "ulice"; Slovak uses "ulica".
Slovak has ä, ĺ, ľ, ô and ŕ, which Czech lacks.
A circumflex on o (ô) means Slovakia.
The letter ñ is common in Spanish, as in España and Logroño.
Spanish uses "calle" for street; Portuguese uses "rua".
Portuguese uses ã, õ and ç, as in Guimarães and estação.
Portuguese uses "rua" for street and "saída" for exit.
Swedish uses ä and ö, as in Göteborg and Malmö.
Swedish street names often end in -gatan, e.g. Storgatan.
Norwegian uses ø and æ with å, but no ä or ö.
Norwegian street names often end in -gata or -veien.
Danish uses ø, æ and å, but no ä or ö.
Danish street names end in -gade or -vej.
Kangaroo, wombat and koala warning signs mean Australia.
Aboriginal-derived place names such as Wagga Wagga point to Australia.
A kiwi warning sign means New Zealand.
Māori place names such as Rotorua and Whanganui point to New Zealand.
Thailand drives on the left; Cambodia drives on the right.
Thai script is rounder and less stacked than Khmer.
Cambodia drives on the right; Thailand drives on the left.
Khmer script stacks subscript consonants and looks more ornate than Thai.
Palafitas (stilt houses) and river boats point to the Norte.
The Norte holds seven states and is the largest region by area, mostly Amazon rainforest.
Manaus and Belém are the big cities; expect heavy rainforest and wide rivers.
Dry thorny scrub and cacti mean the sertão of the Nordeste.
Nine states make up the Nordeste, with long palm-lined beaches along the Atlantic.
Colonial Baroque towns such as Salvador are in the Nordeste.
Brasília and its modernist buildings are in the Distrito Federal, inside this region.
The Pantanal wetland lies largely in Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul.
The region is made up of Goiás, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul and the Distrito Federal.
The Sudeste has four states: São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo.
Minas Gerais has the colonial gold-mining towns, such as Ouro Preto.
It holds the largest cities and the most populous part of the country.
The Sul has three states: Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
Araucaria pines, German half-timbered houses and Italian vineyards point to the Sul.
The Sul has the coldest winters in Brazil, and frost is common.
The first digit groups the states: 1x is São Paulo, 2x is Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and 3x is Minas Gerais.
4x covers Paraná (41-46) and Santa Catarina (47-49), 5x is Rio Grande do Sul, and 6x covers the Centre-West plus Tocantins, Acre and Rondônia.
7x is Bahia plus Sergipe (79), 8x is the rest of the Nordeste, and 9x is Pará, Amazonas, Roraima, Amapá and Maranhão.
The x1 code is usually the main city of each group: 11 São Paulo, 21 Rio de Janeiro, 31 Belo Horizonte, 41 Curitiba, 51 Porto Alegre, 61 Brasília, 71 Salvador, 81 Recife and 91 Belém.
Since 2018 Brazil uses Mercosur plates in the ABC1D23 format, with a blue band on top.
The older Brazilian grey plates read ABC-1234, with the city and state written above.
Portuguese words like "Pare", "Lombada" and "Pedágio" separate Brazil from its Spanish-speaking neighbours.
Light blue-white-light blue horizontal with the Sun of May in the centre.
White over red with a blue square at the hoist holding one white star.
Yellow double-width, then blue, then red. Ecuador has the same bands plus a coat of arms.
Vertical red-white-red. Canada is similar but with a maple leaf and a wider white centre.
Red-yellow-green horizontal, with a coat of arms on the state flag.
Yellow double-width, blue, red, with a coat of arms in the centre. Colombia has no emblem.
Nine blue and white stripes with a sun in the white canton. Greece has a cross there instead.
Red-white-blue horizontal with a different emblem on each side.
Vertical light blue-white-light blue with a coat of arms. Argentina is horizontal.
Blue-white-red-white-blue with a double-width red centre. Thailand has a double-width blue centre.
Quartered white, red, blue, white with a blue star on white and a red star on blue.
A white cross dividing blue and red quarters, with a coat of arms showing an open Bible.
Red and white stripes with a blue triangle at the hoist holding a white star.
Blue field with a yellow horizontal stripe low down and two white stars in the upper hoist.
White over red halves with a counter-coloured disc, red over white, offset toward the hoist.
Union Jack, a large Commonwealth Star and a Southern Cross of five white stars. New Zealand has four red stars.
Union Jack and a Southern Cross of four red stars edged in white. Australia has five white stars.
Dark blue field with a red border and a central oval showing a beach scene with a palm tree.
Blue field with a white star over a grey latte stone, within a flower wreath.
Blue field with a white triangle edged in red, holding a bald eagle with a staff and club.
Bengali letters hang from a horizontal bar along the top, as in ঢাকা (Dhaka).
Bengali is also written in India (West Bengal), so the script alone does not rule India out; ঢাকা is Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh.
Lao is closely related to Thai but its letters are simpler, with fewer loops and no headline-style flourishes.
ວຽງຈັນ is Vientiane, the capital of Laos.
